sens: one who opposes Christ by claiming to replace or counterfeit Him
the spirit of falsehood and denial that refuses to acknowledge Jesus as the Christ
one who denies that Jesus has come in the flesh
one who denies the Father and the Son
G0500.detail: 1. The antichrist is primarily a figure or character who claims to take the place of Christ, usurping His authority. The Greek word is composed of "anti" (against, in place of) and "Christ": it refers to one who replaces Christ or opposes Him. John speaks of an expected coming of this major antichrist (1 John 2:18). 2. However, John broadens the meaning: the antichrist is not just a future person, but also a spirit, a force of falsehood already active in the world (1 John 4:3). This spirit drives people to deny the truth of Jesus and spread lies about His nature. 3. The antichrist is characterized by the refusal to confess that Jesus has come in the flesh, that is, by the refusal to acknowledge His real incarnation (2 John 1:7). It is a rejection of the central event of salvation. 4. Fundamentally, the antichrist denies the Father and the Son: it rejects both the identity of Jesus and His relationship to the Father (1 John 2:22). It is a radical lie about who God is.
G0500.origine: The Greek word ἀντίχριστος is composed of two elements: "anti" means "against" or "in place of," and "christos" means "anointed," designating the Messiah. The word appears only in the letters of John, where it refers both to an expected eschatological figure and a spirit of falsehood present from then on. The idea of opposition to Christ cloaked in pretense goes back to Jesus' warnings about false christs and false prophets (Matthew 24:24).
G0500.emploi: The word "antichrist" appears only four times in the New Testament, exclusively in the letters of John (1 John 2:18, 2:22, 4:3, and 2 John 1:7). John informs his readers that although the great antichrist is expected at the end of times, there are already many antichrists present, manifesting the same spirit of denial (1 John 2:18). This spirit is characterized by three refusals: to deny that Jesus is the Christ (2:22), to deny the incarnation of Jesus (2 John 1:7), and to refuse to confess Jesus (4:3). John insists that his readers recognize these false teachers and this spiritual lie, for antichristianity is not a distant threat but a present reality within the Church itself.
G0500.portee: For the Christian, this word invites vigilance against teachings that deny Jesus or the Father. The antichrist is not primarily a distant political figure, but the spirit of falsehood that opposes the truth of Christ within the Church. Recognizing the antichrist means discerning false teachings and remaining steadfast in the confession of Jesus as the incarnate Savior and Son of the Father.

sens: To draw water from a well or spring
To perform the action of drawing and carrying water
G0501.detail:
1. The verb designates the concrete action of drawing water from a well, spring, or reservoir. It is the ordinary, everyday gesture observed when someone lowers a bucket to bring up water. At the wedding in Cana, Jesus tells the servants: "Draw now" (John 2:8), meaning fill the jars from a source or well, and they carry it to the master of the feast. This action is so obvious that it is referred to simply by the verb without a complement: "absol.", as grammar states.
2. By extension, the word evokes the entirety of the labor: not only drawing the water but carrying it to the place where it will be used. When Jesus tells the Samaritan woman, "you will no longer come here to draw" (John 4:15), He suggests that she will be spared the daily and tiring trip to the well. The word thus embodies ordinary work, toil, and even the thirst that continually brings one back to the well.
G0501.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἄντλος (antlos), which referred to stagnant water, the bilge water drawn from the bottom of a ship's hold. The verb thus primarily means "to bail out" (to empty water from the bottom). From there, it took on the general meaning of "drawing water" from any source. In the Hebrew of the Greek Old Testament, it often translates שָׁאַב (sha'ab), which has exactly the same meaning: to draw water from the well.
G0501.emploi: The verb appears four times, all in the Gospel of John, and only in the concrete sense: to draw water. At the wedding in Cana (John 2:8-9), Jesus commands to draw water from the empty jars; the servants do so and bring it to the master, who discovers that the water has become wine. To the Samaritan woman (John 4:7, 15), Jesus asks her for a drink, and she replies that she hopes not to have to come to draw anymore thanks to the living water He promised to give. The word remains attached to the material reality: it is physical water, physical labor, but John uses it as a sign of spiritual thirst and God's gift.
G0501.portee: This humble word reminds us that the Gospel of John often speaks of water as an image: the water drawn from the well represents always provisional human satisfaction; the water that Jesus gives is the gift of the Holy Spirit that truly quenches thirst. For the reader, "to draw" suggests labor, thirst, dependence on the everyday, all that Jesus comes to transform. It is a word that also evokes prayer: we draw from God as from an inexhaustible source.

sens: a container used to draw water
the action or means of drawing
G0502.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a bucket or container used to draw water from a well. In John 4:11, the Samaritan woman is surprised that Jesus, without a bucket, can draw this "living water" He speaks of: she thinks of the necessary material equipment to bring water up from the deep well.
2. By extension, the word can also refer to the action of drawing itself, the technical means of drawing water from the well—the equipment or instrument essential for accessing the deep water resource.
G0502.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « antléō » (ἀντλέω), which literally means "to draw, to pull." It designates the object used for this action: the bucket or container. The original image is that of daily work in a region where water must be extracted from wells, a reality well known in the Mediterranean and Oriental world of the time.
G0502.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 4:11. It is a concrete, practical term that evokes the ordinary life of a well and its material conditions. The Samaritan woman uses it to highlight the material obstacle: Jesus does not have the bucket that any ordinary man must possess to draw. This unique usage reveals its narrative role: to highlight the contrast between the ordinary and insufficient means of man (a bucket) and the extraordinary gift of Jesus (the living water that springs up to eternal life).
G0502.portee: This simple detail of the bucket reveals how Jesus addresses the woman where she is: in her concrete and material needs. But He invites her to see beyond. The contrast between the ordinary bucket and the living water teaches that what God offers far exceeds what we can procure by our own means. It is a lesson on the sufficiency of God's gift compared to the insufficiency of our efforts.

sens: Who refuses to submit to authority
Who does not recognize established power or rule
Disobedient, insubordinate
Who escapes control or order
G0506.detail: 1. The word describes a person or thing that refuses to submit to authority: in 1 Timothy 1:9, Paul classifies "rebels" among those for whom the law exists, alongside the ungodly and sinners — these are people who actively reject the established order. 2. It characterizes one who does not recognize legitimate power: in Titus 1:6 and 1:10, the apostle speaks of "rebellious" people in the churches, individuals who refuse to submit to apostolic teaching and discipline, sowing confusion among believers. 3. The word can also apply to things that escape order: in Hebrews 2:8, the text states that "all things" are not yet "subject" to Christ, meaning that the current world remains partially rebellious to His authority, contrary to the divine promise.
G0506.origine: The Greek word is formed from the negation "a-" (meaning "not") and the verb "hypotassô" (to submit, to arrange under). Literally, it means "not submitted." The root evokes the image of a troop or an object that cannot be placed under authority, which refuses to be put in order. The word belongs to the same family as "submission" and "subordinate" — it is their opposite.
G0506.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, only in Paul’s writings and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. In 1 Timothy 1:9, it refers to hardened sinners to whom the law must apply. In Titus 1:6 and 1:10, it characterizes troublemakers who oppose the order of the local church. In Hebrews 2:8, used in the passive form ("subjected"), it expresses the eschatological subjection of all things to Christ — the contrast between the promise and present reality. The context is always that of legitimate authority facing resistance or failure.
G0506.portee: This word reminds Christians that rebellion against established order — whether political, familial, or ecclesiastical — is incompatible with faith and the law of God. It invites self-examination: am I submitted or do I remain rebellious? It also shows that the current world, although ordered by Christ, still awaits its complete submission — a perspective that strengthens hope in His glorious return.

sens: Upward, in an ascending vertical direction
The top, the upper part of something
Above, in the heavenly or spiritual realm
What belongs to the divine or eternal domain
G0507.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial and vertical: to go up, to rise. When Jesus turns to His Father in prayer, He "lifts His eyes up" (John 11:41), a natural gesture that shows an orientation of the soul toward heaven.
2. In the sense of "the upper part of an object": the servants fill the jars "to the brim," to the top, to the summit of the container (John 2:7).
3. In a spiritual and metaphysical sense: Jesus says "I am from above" (John 8:23) to indicate that He comes from heaven, from the domain of God, while His interlocutors are "from below," attached to this world. This is the opposition between the eternal and the earthly.
4. Used with the definite article, the word regularly designates the heavenly or divine realm: "the Jerusalem above" (Galatians 4:26) is the community of God's children in heaven; "the things above" (Colossians 3:1-2) refer to the eternal realities that the believer must seek.
G0507.origine: The word comes from the preposition ἀνά (ana, "from below to above") which expresses upward movement. It is an adverb derived from an ancient root related to the idea of lifting, elevating. In biblical Greek, ἄνω regularly translates the Hebrew מַעְלָה (maalah, "height, what is upward"), particularly in expressions of spiritual or heavenly direction.
G0507.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. It is first used in a spatial and concrete sense: looking up (John 11:41), filling a jar to the top (John 2:7), seeing signs in the sky (Acts 2:19). But its usage gradually becomes more theological: it designates the domain of God, heaven, the eternal. Particularly in Paul, "from above" becomes a spiritual invitation: the believer must seek the things above (Colossians 3:1), aspire to the heavenly calling (Philippians 3:14). John makes it a marker of Jesus' divine origin in relation to the earthly world (John 8:23). It is a humble yet rich word that unites the concrete and the spiritual.
G0507.portee: This word invites Christians to direct their gaze and hearts toward God and eternal realities. Used in calls to prayer or spiritual aspiration, it reminds us that our true homeland is not here below, but in heaven. It also helps to understand that Jesus does not come from this world, but is sent from the heavenly Father. It is a heart orientation that every believer is called to share.

sens: Room located on the upper floor of a house
Place for solemn meetings or meals
G0508.detail:
1. The word literally designates a room or living space located above the ground floor, in the upper part of a house. It is an upper room, generally spacious and well-furnished. In Mark 14:15 and Luke 22:12, it refers to a large furnished room ready to host an important meal.
2. By extension, this term evokes a space reserved for solemn or intimate moments: it is in an upper room that Jesus gathers His disciples for the Passover meal, the moment when He institutes the Lord's Supper. The word thus takes on a nuance of gravity and spiritual intimacy.
G0508.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "ana" (upward, ascending) and "gê" (the earth). Literally, it means "that which rises from the earth" or "that which is above the ground." It is a simple and concrete image: the room that rises, that is elevated. This reflects the geography of ancient Near Eastern houses, where main rooms were added upward.
G0508.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two parallel accounts of Mark and Luke. Both times, it refers to the upper room in Jerusalem where Jesus and His twelve apostles celebrate the Last Passover together. It is a place presented as large, well-furnished, and prepared in advance — a space worthy of receiving this pivotal moment. The term remains simple and factual: the emphasis is not on the word itself, but on the event that takes place there, the institution of the Lord's Supper.
G0508.portee: This upper room is the setting for Jesus' last meal with His disciples, a foundational moment of the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper according to Christian traditions. It symbolizes a place of intimacy where Jesus entrusts His spiritual testament to His apostles. For the reader, this term reminds us that the central events of faith do not always unfold in public places, but in intimate and communal settings.

sens: from the top down, from the upper part to the lower part
from heaven, from God who is above all
from the beginning, from the origin
again, a second time
G0509.detail:
1. The spatial and physical sense: "from above" refers to what comes from the upper part, from the top down. It literally describes what descends from above: the temple veil in Matthew 27:51 was torn "from top to bottom," just as Jesus' tunic was woven "from top to bottom" (John 19:23).
2. The spiritual and heavenly sense: when John speaks of the one "who comes from above" (John 3:31), it is no longer just a simple physical direction, but a divine origin, from heaven. This wisdom that "comes from above" (James 3:15) is that of God, opposed to earthly and fleshly wisdom.
3. The temporal and original sense: the expression can also mean "from the beginning," "from the start," as when Luke says he composed his account having "carefully investigated everything from the beginning" (Luke 1:3). It conveys the idea of continuity from the origins.
4. The iterative sense: "again," "once more." Jesus asks Nicodemus if he can "be born again" (John 3:3) — not a new birth after the first, but a completely new birth from above, which entirely transforms existence.
G0509.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἄνω (anō), which means "upward" or "above." The adverb ἄνωθεν adds the suffix -θεν which marks origin or source, hence the literal meaning "from [the part] above." It is an ancient compound word that combines the idea of direction (upward) and source (from where it comes). In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew term for what is elevated or heavenly.
G0509.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels, particularly in John. Its uses can be divided into three groups: first, the raw spatial sense (the temple veil, the tunic), very concrete; then the spiritual sense dominated by John, where "from above" means "from heaven," "from God" (John 3:31, 19:11, James 1:17, 3:15, 3:17); finally, the less frequent temporal or iterative sense (Luke 1:3, Acts 26:5 for "long ago," John 3:3, 3:7, Galatians 4:9 for "again"). The nuance changes depending on the context: spatial in Matthew and Mark, theological in John and James, temporal in Luke and Paul.
G0509.portee: This word introduces a major biblical distinction: there are two worlds, two sources of wisdom and authority, one from above (heavenly, divine) and the other earthly. For John, being "born from above" is the condition to see the kingdom of God — it is not a simple improvement, but a radical transformation of existence. For James, the wisdom from above is recognized by its fruits (it is "pure, peaceable, gentle"), while earthly wisdom breeds jealousy and disorder. This word invites the reader to discern their sources of inspiration and to seek what truly comes from God.

sens: located in the upper part of a region, inland
elevated in altitude or importance
G0510.detail:
1. The word describes what is geographically situated upward, the interior or inland part of a region. Acts 19:1 speaks of the "high provinces" of Asia, meaning the inland lands, towards the Anatolian plateau, as opposed to the Mediterranean coasts. It is a matter of direction and relative position in space.
2. By extension, the word can also qualify what is elevated or superior in dignity or rank, but this figurative use is clearly expressed only once in the New Testament.
G0510.origine: The word comes from ἀνώτερος (anōteros), which means "superior" or "higher" (derived from ἄνω, anō, "up, upward"). It is a comparative adjective. The root evokes the idea of movement or position upward, towards what is elevated. The suffix -ικός makes it a relational or qualitative adjective.
G0510.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:1, where Paul travels through the "high provinces" of Asia Minor before arriving in Ephesus. The geographical context is clear: it refers to the elevated inland lands of the region, different from the coastal or lower areas. This unique use shows how the adjective applies to territorial regions to specify their relative location.
G0510.portee: This word reminds the reader how God guided the apostle Paul through the unpredictable paths of Asia Minor to ultimately lead him to Ephesus, a major center of the Greek world. It illustrates the progression of God's plan and the mobility required for the Gospel mission in the first century.

sens: To a place located at a higher altitude, ascending.
To a place of greater dignity or honor.
Previously, earlier in a text.
G0511.detail:
1. The word describes a movement upward or a high position: "go to the last place, so that… he may say to you: Friend, go up higher" (Luke 14:10). Jesus literally speaks of ascending to a better place at the table.

2. By extension, "higher" signifies a position of greater honor or dignity: in the same verse, going higher means receiving a place of honor "in front of all those who are at the table."

3. The word can also refer to what precedes in a text or discourse, in the sense of "before" or "previously": "After saying first" (Hebrews 10:8) introduces a prior citation from Scripture.
G0511.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "upward." It is a comparative adjective (like "greater," "smaller"): it places something at a higher degree. Greek often uses place adjectives in a figurative sense to express honor, dignity, or the logical order of a text.
G0511.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 14:10, Jesus uses it in a parable about humility: the one who takes the last place will be invited to go higher. In Hebrews 10:8, it is used in a temporal sense to refer to an earlier passage of Scripture. In both cases, the context plays on order and honor: social and spatial in Luke, logical and textual in Hebrews.
G0511.portee: This word of Jesus in Luke 14:10 teaches that humility and reserve are the authentic paths to true honor. It overturns the wisdom of the world: it is not by pushing oneself upward that one achieves true dignity, but by accepting the last place. For the believer, it invites an attitude of trust in God rather than in one's own efforts for recognition.

sens: That produces no profit or advantage
That serves no purpose, which is vain or barren
That brings no spiritual or moral benefit
G0512.detail:
1. The word designates what yields nothing, what is not beneficial: a "useless" discussion builds nothing or no one, as Paul explains to Titus by warning against genealogical disputes that serve no purpose (Titus 3:9).
2. More broadly, it refers to what is vain or barren, incapable of producing a lasting result. The old Mosaic ordinance, rendered useless by the work of Christ, illustrates this: it could not accomplish what it existed for (Hebrews 7:18).
3. Uselessness suggests a complete absence of value or spiritual yield: something that consumes time and energy without enriching faith or transforming the heart.
G0512.origine: The Greek word is composed of the negative "a" and "ôphelos," which means profit or advantage. It literally means "without profit." The root evokes the idea of bearing or bringing something: what bears no fruit is useless. This term appears in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) to translate the Hebrew "ya'al" (to serve no purpose) in Isaiah and Jeremiah.
G0512.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. Paul uses it in Titus 3:9 to describe genealogical discussions and disputes of the law: not that they are false, but they build nothing in faith and can even divide the Church. In Hebrews 7:18, the term refers to the old priestly ordinance: it was good in its time, but it proved powerless to accomplish salvation, hence its abolition. In both cases, it is a judgment on effectiveness, not on morality.
G0512.portee: This word reminds Christians of the importance of discerning what truly builds faith from what diverts it. It invites not to waste spiritual energy on quarrels or traditions that do not produce justice and peace. It is also an invitation to recognize the perfection of Christ's sacrifice: where the old law was vain, Christ accomplished what no human ordinance could do.

sens: cutting tool used to chop wood
figuratively: imminent and merciless judgment
G0513.detail:
1. The axe is a tool with a sharp blade attached to a wooden handle, intended for felling trees or splitting wood. John the Baptist uses it as an image: "The axe is already laid at the root of the trees" (Matthew 3:10).
2. John employs the axe to announce a divine judgment that strikes without delay and without exception. The tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire. The tool is laid at the root, ready to act: judgment is imminent and certain.
G0513.origine: The Greek word axinē refers to the common working instrument in the Mediterranean world for chopping wood. It translates the Hebrew garzen or kardom ("axe," "hatchet"). The image of divine judgment as a blade ready to cut down the bad tree belongs to the prophetic language of the Old Testament.
G0513.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two parallel passages where John the Baptist announces the baptism of repentance: Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9. In these two identical verses, John does not use the axe to speak of ordinary work, but as an eschatological metaphor for divine judgment. The axe is already laid at the root, which means that judgment is imminent and inevitable: each tree (each person) will be evaluated according to its fruits, and whoever does not produce good fruits will be cut off.
G0513.portee: John the Baptist's axe reminds believers that judgment is not far off: it is now that the decision is made, now that life produces its fruits or lack of fruits. The image invites vigilance and immediate conversion, for grace precedes certain judgment.

sens: Having weight, value, or importance
Deserving something, whether good or bad
Appropriate, suitable, fitting
Esteemed worthy of honor or respect
G0514.detail:
1. The word first evokes the idea of weight and value: something that truly "weighs," that matters. Romans 8:18 uses it when Paul says that present sufferings are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come — they do not have the same weight.

2. "Worthy" also means "deserving" — for good or for ill. For good: the prodigal son considers himself "unworthy" to be called a son (Luke 15:21), or the apostle John acknowledges that he is not worthy to untie the sandals of Jesus (John 1:27). For ill: Romans 1:32 states that those who do such things "deserve" death.

3. The word also designates what is appropriate, suitable, or fitting. Matthew 3:8 asks for fruits "worthy" of repentance — acts that truly correspond to this change of heart. Similarly, Acts 26:20 speaks of "works worthy of repentance."

4. Finally, "worthy" applies to one who is esteemed worthy of honor: the laborer is worthy of his wages (Luke 10:7), and in Revelation 4:11 the Lamb is worthy to receive honor and glory.
G0514.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to weigh" or "to have weight." This image of weight explains the meaning well: what is worthy is what "weighs" enough to deserve something, or what has enough value to be suitable. The family of the word includes other terms related to balance and measure. In Hebrew, the word בֵּן ("son") sometimes has this nuance of suitability or relation; in biblical Hebrew, שָׁוָה means "equal" or "appropriate."
G0514.emploi: The word appears 39 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels, Acts, and Revelation. It is used in both good and bad senses. In a good sense, it often designates one who deserves a reward or honor: the laborer worthy of his wages, those who will walk with the Lord in white garments because they are worthy (Revelation 3:4), or the Lamb worthy to receive glory and honor (Revelation 5:9, 12). In a bad sense, it speaks of one who deserves punishment: Acts 25:11 refers to a crime worthy of death. The word is also used to express suitability: fruits worthy of repentance (Matthew 3:8, Luke 3:8), works that correspond to repentance (Acts 26:20). Sometimes it is absolute, implying a relation: in the wedding feast of Matthew 22:8, the invited guests were not worthy, without needing to specify worthy of what.
G0514.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on their value before God and the conformity of their life. Am I worthy? Not in the sense of deserving salvation by my works — none are — but in the sense of producing fruits that truly "correspond" to the repentance and faith I confess. It is a call to authenticity: may my conduct be worthy of my commitment to Christ.

sens: To estimate that someone deserves something
To think that someone is worthy of receiving an honor, a reward, or special treatment
To believe that someone is suitable for a task or mission
To consider as appropriate or fitting
G0515.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of an evaluation: one judges that someone has the merit or value required for something. It is an act of discernment, coming from one who has the authority to decide. For example, in Hebrews 3:3, the Father has "judged worthy" the Son of a glory greater than that of Moses, recognizing Him as worthy of a greater honor.
2. The word is also used for the rewards and punishments that people deserve. In 2 Thessalonians 1:11, Paul prays that God will judge the believers worthy of their heavenly calling. Conversely, in Hebrews 10:29, he asks what "worse punishment" will be judged worthy for one who rejects the Son of God — one who deserves it.
3. It can express suitability or appropriateness: to believe that an action or a person fits the situation. In Acts 15:38, Paul judges it more suitable not to take Mark with him, considering it inappropriate after his previous departure.
4. Finally, it is used for the humble recognition of not deserving something. In Luke 7:7, the centurion says to Jesus: "I did not consider myself worthy to go in person to you," acknowledging his unworthiness.
G0515.origine: The word comes from the adjective ἄξιος (axios, "worthy"), which designates what has weight, value, or deserves a favorable judgment. The verb adds the action of judging or estimating. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, verbs like בָּקַשׁ (bâqash, "to ask, seek") or בְּעָא (be'â, "to ask") express a judgment of value and a request. The basic idea is that of a balance: one weighs the qualities of someone to see if they balance the price of a reward or honor.
G0515.emploi: The verb appears seven times in the New Testament, mainly in the Pauline and Hebrew epistles. In Luke 7:7, the centurion uses it to express his humility before Jesus. In Acts 15:38 and 28:22, Paul or the apostles use it to express practical suitability. In 2 Thessalonians 1:11, it is God who judges the believers worthy of their calling. In 1 Timothy 5:17 and Hebrews 3:3, it involves recognizing the dignity of someone: the elders who lead well, and Christ worthy of a greater glory. In Hebrews 10:29, the context is that of deserved punishment. The word nuances according to the subject: a man who judges his own unworthiness (Luke), God who recognizes the dignity of a person or a calling, or the worst consequences of despising the Son.
G0515.portee: This word teaches two essential truths for the Christian. First, the awareness of our natural unworthiness: we deserve nothing by ourselves, like the centurion who recognizes himself unworthy of the Lord's presence. Second, it is God alone who judges us worthy — worthy of His love, of His heavenly calling, of His honor — not by our works, but by grace. This calls for recognition and responsibility: if God judges us worthy of a calling, we have the duty to show ourselves worthy of it.

sens: in a way that conforms to the value, rank, or dignity of someone or something
in a way that honors, respects the importance of someone or something
in a deserved, appropriate manner
in a way that corresponds to who one is or what one has received
G0516.detail:
1. The word describes a manner of acting that is commensurate with the person or cause involved. When welcoming someone "in a worthy manner," one gives them the honor and respect they deserve: thus, in Romans 16:2, Phoebe must be received "in a manner worthy of the saints."
2. The word also evokes the idea of deserving or corresponding to something: to walk "in a manner worthy of God" means to live in a way that honors God and befits His majesty (1 Thessalonians 2:12).
3. In practical life, this means conducting oneself with an attitude and actions that reflect the value of what one represents. In Ephesians 4:1, the believer must walk "in a manner worthy of the calling you have received" — that is, let their conduct reflect the divine calling of which they are the object.
4. This word also encompasses conformity: to do something in a manner that corresponds to what is fitting. In 3 John 1:6, providing for the journey "in a manner worthy of God" means doing so with generosity and care that honors God's name.
G0516.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that expresses the notion of value, weight, or importance: ἀξίος (axios, "worthy"). The adverb takes up this image of an action that "weighs" as much as the dignity or value of its object. That is why one says of a person that they are worthy when they have recognized value, a moral weight. In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding idea was expressed by words like כָּבוֹד (kabod, "glory, honor").
G0516.emploi: The adverb ἀξίως appears 6 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Pauline epistles. It always modifies the verb "to walk" or "to conduct oneself" (or an equivalent like "to receive"). Its use revolves around a central ethical question: how to live in accordance with who one is or what one has received? In Romans 16:2, Ephesians 4:1, Philippians 1:27, Colossians 1:10, and 1 Thessalonians 2:12, Paul exhorts believers to live in a worthy manner, whether of their calling, the Gospel, or God Himself. In 3 John 1:6, the same principle applies to Christian hospitality. The adverb is often accompanied by a dative complement ("worthy of God," "worthy of the calling") that specifies what the conduct must correspond to.
G0516.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that conduct is never a matter of whim or indifference: it must correspond to the dignity of the one we serve and the calling we have received. Living "worthily" means allowing one's faith to transform daily life, so that every act reflects the seriousness of God's call. It is an invitation to authenticity and coherence: not to dishonor by one's actions the name of God or the Gospel that one proclaims.

sens: That cannot be seen by the eyes
That escapes perception
That is hidden or concealed
That is spiritual or immaterial
G0517.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very simple: that which cannot be seen by the eyes. It is the opposite of visible. But the word carries an idea of power: the invisible things of God — his eternal power, his divinity — can nonetheless be seen "as if with the eye" in his works (Romans 1:20), so striking they are to those who look.

2. The word also designates what naturally escapes human perception. Jesus is called "the image of the invisible God" (Colossians 1:15): God himself cannot be grasped by our sight, but he has manifested himself in Jesus, his image.

3. In Colossians 1:16, the invisible is contrasted with the visible when speaking of heavenly realities: thrones, dominions, principalities, authorities (angelic powers) are invisible beings, yet just as real as the world we see.

4. By extension, invisible qualifies what is spiritual, immaterial, transcendent. God is called "the only God, invisible" (1 Timothy 1:17): his divine essence cannot be directly contemplated by living man. Moses acted "as seeing him who is invisible" (Hebrews 11:27): by faith, he grasped a reality that no eye can see.
G0517.origine: The Greek word ἀόρατος is composed of the privative prefix α (meaning "not," "without") and ὁράω (to see, to look). Literally, it means "that which cannot be seen." This simple and clear formation was well known to the Greeks to describe anything that escapes sight. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it renders the Hebrew תֹּהוּ (tohu, the formless chaos) and מִסְתָּר (misttar, that which is hidden), showing that the idea of invisibility encompasses both the absence of form and concealment.
G0517.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in contexts of deep theology. It first qualifies the invisible attributes of God (Romans 1:20), of which creation bears witness. It then applies to God the Father himself (Colossians 1:15, 1 Timothy 1:17): it is a title that emphasizes the mystery and divine transcendence. In Colossians 1:16, it designates the heavenly powers, spiritual beings that we do not see but that truly exist. Finally, in Hebrews 11:27, it evokes faith as the ability to grasp the invisible: Moses behaved "as seeing" (persevering) because he saw by faith him whom no one can physically see. The word always aims to awaken the believer's consciousness to a reality that transcends the senses.
G0517.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the deep reality — God, his essence, the power of heavenly realities — is not captive to what the eye sees. It invites cultivating faith not as a weakness, but as a way of seeing rightly. It also affirms the dignity of the spiritual world: the invisible is no less real than the visible; it is even more enduring. For the believer, it is an exhortation not to reduce his faith to what he can touch or measure, but to let his heart open to the hidden power of God that sustains all.

sens: To convey information, a message to someone
To recount what one has seen or heard
To proclaim news, especially the good news of salvation
To bear witness to something or someone
G0518.detail:
1. The basic meaning: to report news, an event, to convey information to someone else. For example, in Matthew 2:8, King Herod asks the Magi to go to Bethlehem and let him know (announce) as soon as they have found the child Jesus. It is to carry information from one point to another.
2. To recount in detail what one has experienced or observed, often vividly. Luke 24:9 recounts how the women "announced" to the disciples all that had happened at the tomb: they report their own experience.
3. To proclaim good news or an important word with the intention of making it known. In 1 Thessalonians 1:9, Paul recalls how the conversion of the Thessalonians was spoken of and how the return of the Lord among them was "announced." It is more than reporting: it is spreading a word of salvation.
4. To bear witness to someone or something, to speak in favor of a person or a reality. Hebrews 2:12 quotes the words of Christ: "I will announce to you," which means "I will proclaim you," "I will make you known" to the assembly.
G0518.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek where the prefix "apo" (ἀπό) means "from, away from, starting from" and "angello" (ἀγγέλλω) means "to carry a message, to announce." The basic idea is that of a messenger who transports news from one place to another: the prefix reinforces the idea of diffusion, of transmission that starts from one point to spread. This Greek word often translates the Hebrew "nagad" (נָגַד) in the active form, which also means "to report, to make known, to declare." The family includes words like "angellos" (messenger, angel) and "angelia" (message, news).
G0518.emploi: The verb "apangellô" appears 47 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. It describes the action of transmitting information: the women announce the resurrection to the disciples (Luke 24:9, Matthew 28:11), Peter announces the Gospel in Acts, John the Baptist has Jesus informed of the miracles that attest to him being the Messiah (Luke 7:22). The word is used for simple information (Acts 12:14: the servant announces that Peter is at the door) and for solemn declarations. Its usage extends from ordinary contexts (reporting news) to spiritual contexts (proclaiming the Gospel), without changing its fundamental meaning: it is always about transmitting what is known from one person to another.
G0518.portee: This word reminds the reader that faith is transmitted by the word, from witness to witness. The women at the tomb, Peter in prison, the disciples: all "announce" what they have seen and known. It is an action verb for the believer: the resurrection of Jesus exists for others only if someone announces it. Every Christian is invited to be the one who reports, who makes known what he has heard and understood about salvation.

sens: to strangle oneself with a rope
to take one's own life by strangulation
to succumb under the weight of guilt (figurative sense)
G0519.detail:
1. The word designates the action of strangling oneself with a rope, in other words, to hang oneself. This is the literal, very concrete sense: one tightens the throat to take one's life. This is exactly what Judas does after betraying Jesus, in Matthew 27:5.

2. In a broader sense, the word can also mean to suffocate or choke, but in the New Testament, the Segond only renders it as "to hang oneself."

3. The text of Matthew suggests a deeper figurative sense: Judas's death is not just a physical act. It expresses the consequence of betrayal and overwhelming remorse — the weight of guilt that morally suffocates him and drives him to the fatal act.
G0519.origine: The Greek word comes from the root ἄγχω ("to press," "to strangle"), which evokes the idea of tightening and suffocation. The prefix ἀπό ("away from," "to the side") reinforces the meaning: it is an act that takes place away from the eyes, in secret, a definitive rupture. In the middle-passive form (as here), the word takes on a reflexive value: not "to strangle someone," but "to strangle oneself."
G0519.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: Matthew 27:5, the account of Judas's death. After delivering Jesus for thirty pieces of silver and witnessing his judgment, Judas is seized with remorse. He throws the coins back into the temple and goes out. Alone, haunted by his betrayal, he chooses to end his life by suicide. Matthew uses this precise Greek term, which underscores both the brutal physical act and the state of moral despair that leads to it.
G0519.portee: This word confronts the reader with a serious spiritual question: that of remorse without repentance, of guilt that paralyzes instead of turning towards God. Judas sees his crime and suffers deeply from it, but instead of seeking forgiveness, he chooses self-destruction. It is a warning: true repentance is not despair, but a return to God and his grace.

sens: To lead someone from one place to another, guiding or physically pulling them along
To lead to a place of judgment, detention, or punishment
To direct a path or route toward a destination
G0520.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to lead or guide someone from one place to another: it is the action of moving someone along with oneself. Jesus says that the broad way leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13-14), like a guide who leads travelers to their destination.

2. The word takes on a judicial and dramatic meaning in the Passion narratives: to take Jesus to the high priest (Matthew 26:57), then to lead him to crucifixion (Matthew 27:31), which describes the action of leading someone to judgment and death. It is a verb of authority: the one who takes has control over the one being taken.

3. In an ordinary context, it means to lead someone (or an animal) to a place: to lead an ox to drink at the well on the Sabbath (Luke 13:15). The verb simply describes the act of guiding someone from point A to point B.
G0520.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἀπό ("away," "aside") and the verb ἄγω ("to lead, to bring"). Literally, it means "to lead away" or "to take away." In Hebrew, it translates verbs like נָהַג ("to lead") and הָלַךְ in the causative form ("to cause to go"). The preposition ἀπό reinforces the idea that the one being led is moving away from their starting point.
G0520.emploi: The verb appears 17 times in the New Testament, notably in the Gospel accounts. It is used in its common concrete sense (leading an animal, Luke 13:15), but it carries particular weight in the Passion narrative, where it repeatedly denotes the action of taking Jesus before the religious and Roman authorities (Matthew 26:57, Mark 14:53, Luke 22:66) or to the cross (Matthew 27:31). Acts uses it to describe the arrest and detention of apostles (Acts 23:17, 24:7, 12:19). Paul also uses it to evoke how the Gentiles, before their conversion, were led without discernment to idols (1 Corinthians 12:2). The context varies, but the core meaning remains: to lead someone to a place or a destiny.
G0520.portee: This verb reminds the reader of the reality of Jesus' leading to the cross: not an accident, but a determined progression from one stage to another of judgment and suffering. It also shows how humans can be led by forces or ideas that blind them—toward destruction like on a path paved with intentions. For the believer, recognizing how one is "led" (by sin, by passions, or by the Spirit) becomes a matter of conscience and discernment.

sens: That produces no result, no fruit
That is devoid of instruction, ignorant
That has not received education, uneducated
G0521.detail:
1. The word first designates what produces nothing good, what is sterile: a useless discussion leads nowhere, it does not build up. In 2 Timothy 2:23, Paul calls to avoid "foolish and useless discussions"—these are quarrels that serve no purpose, that do not strengthen faith.

2. The word also carries the idea of lack of instruction: the one who is useless has not received the necessary teaching, they act without knowledge or discernment. It is ignorance that renders a word hollow.

3. More broadly, it is the absence of education, moral or intellectual training: someone useless has remained raw, without being trained in reflection or wisdom.
G0521.origine: The word comes from the Greek παιδεύω (paideúô), "to instruct, to educate, to train"—especially training children (παῖς, paîs). The prefix ἀ- signifies negation: it literally means "without education." The starting image is that of a child who has not been raised, who has not learned. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew notion of "fool," one who lacks wisdom.
G0521.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:23. Paul uses it to qualify the "foolish and useless discussions" that the servant of the Lord must avoid. These debates are useless because they build nothing: instead of edifying faith, they generate quarrels and divisions. It is a call to pastoral prudence: it is better to refrain from sterile controversies and focus on what truly instructs in faith.
G0521.portee: This word warns us of the importance of distinguishing, in our faith life, what bears fruit from what merely disperses our energies. Groundless discussions, quarrels over secondary points, debates that sink rather than uplift—all of this is useless. Paul invites us to wisdom: to cultivate what edifies, what builds, what truly instructs.

sens: To take away or withdraw something in a way that separates it from its place or from what held it
In the passive voice, to be taken away or separated from someone or something
G0522.detail:
1. The verb denotes the action of lifting, raising something to move it away or make it disappear—it is a physical removal or withdrawal. In everyday life, it is like taking an object from its place.

2. In the passive voice (the form used in the Bible), it means to be taken away or torn from someone. Jesus tells the disciples that the days will come when "the bridegroom will be taken away from them" (Matthew 9:15): the bridegroom, who is with them, will be taken from them, separated by death or absence. It is the image of a painful separation, which explains why they will fast then.
G0522.origine: The word is formed from the preposition "apo" (away, out of) and the verb "airō" (to lift, to raise). The starting image is that of lifting something to remove it, to raise it and set it aside. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb "nasaʿ," which means "to depart, to go away" and also evokes the idea of lifting or raising.
G0522.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the passive voice and always in the first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, and Luke). In all three cases, it refers to the same scene: Jesus responds to a question about fasting by saying that his disciples will fast when the bridegroom—himself, in symbolic language—will be taken away from them. The usage is therefore uniform and metaphorical: the "removal" of the bridegroom figures the moment when Jesus will be separated from his disciples by his death and ascension.
G0522.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus' departure was a real separation, not a fiction. It was painful for the disciples, legitimizing their mourning symbolized by fasting. But it is not definitive: fasting has an end, as Jesus promised his return and resurrection. It is a word of realism and hope.

sens: Ask for something to be returned that has been taken from you or that is owed to you
Demand the reimbursement or restitution of what has been given or lent
In a figurative sense, ask for an account, withdraw or reclaim
G0523.detail:
1. The word evokes the act of asking for the return of what belongs to you and is held by another: in Luke 6:30, it literally refers to claiming a possession that someone has taken, but Jesus instead invites not to do so, to give without seeking to recover.
2. It also means to demand the reimbursement of what has been entrusted or lent — to ask for an account or the return of what has been committed, like a creditor who demands his due again.
3. In a broader and figurative sense, it is to withdraw or reclaim what one had entrusted to someone: in Luke 12:20, God "demands back" the soul of the rich man, meaning He takes it back, like one retrieves a deposit.
G0523.origine: The word is formed from the prefix ἀπό (apo, "back") and the verb αἰτέω (aiteō, "to ask"). The basic image is that of asking for something to be returned, claiming something one wants to see come back to oneself. It is an insistent request, marked by the desire to recover or reclaim.
G0523.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke. In Luke 6:30, Jesus uses it to invite the disciple to detach his heart from material goods: not to claim what has been taken or given, to accept loss. In Luke 12:20, it takes on an existential and dramatic meaning: God "demands back" the soul of the foolish rich man — it is the withdrawal of life itself, the call back to God. Both uses reveal that the word touches on what is precious and that one wants to keep: money, possessions, life.
G0523.portee: This word questions the believer about their relationship to possession: are we ready to let go of our goods without claiming them back, as Jesus teaches? It also reminds us that nothing truly belongs to us — that our very life is lent to us and that God can demand it back at any moment. It is an invitation to detachment and humility in the face of what passes away.

sens: cease to feel pain
become insensitive, hard-hearted
renounce all morality
G0524.detail: 1. Literally, the word means "to no longer feel pain": it is the idea of someone who, after suffering for a long time, ends up being touched by nothing. 2. Figuratively, it describes the hardening of the heart and conscience: one who "has lost all feeling" (Ephesians 4:19) is no longer capable of feeling shame, guilt, or disgust towards evil. Their heart has become like dead. 3. This moral insensitivity drives the person to abandon themselves recklessly to impurity and all sins, because they no longer feel any inner discomfort or restraint.
G0524.origine: The Greek word is composed of the prefix ἀπό ("away from") and the verb ἀλγέω ("to suffer, to feel pain"). The basic image is that of a person who moves away from pain, who ceases to feel it. In ancient Greek, Thucydides uses it in the strict sense of "to stop suffering." But by the time of the New Testament, the meaning has broadened to denote moral and spiritual insensitivity, a complete hardening of the conscience.
G0524.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 4:19. Paul describes there the path of moral degradation taken by one who strays from the Gospel: first, they lose their moral sensitivity (they "have lost all feeling"), then they give themselves without restraint to impurity. This word depicts the ultimate stage of a progressive hardening: it is not a sudden fall, but the culmination of a long indifference to the voice of God.
G0524.portee: This word warns us of the danger of gradual hardening: when one voluntarily closes their eyes to sin, when one ignores the conviction of the Spirit, they risk gradually losing all spiritual sensitivity. The heart can become so hard that it no longer feels guilt or the need to be saved. It is a call to keep a lively and receptive conscience towards God.

sens: Remove, distance something or someone from a place or situation
Free oneself, detach from someone or something
Be free, free oneself from an obligation to someone
G0525.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of removing or distancing: Jesus healed the sick whose unclean spirits were released from them (Acts 19:12) — they left these people to go away.
2. It also means to free oneself, to detach oneself: the Messiah was to deliver all those who through fear of death were held in slavery (Hebrews 2:15).
3. In a judicial context, it means to become free from someone, to settle a matter with them. Jesus advises the debtor pressed by his creditor: "make an effort on the way to release yourself from him" (Luke 12:58), meaning arrange to no longer owe him before arriving before the judge.
G0525.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "apo" (away from) and the verb "allassô" (to change, to exchange, to defer). The primary image is that of separating from, detaching from, putting at a distance. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates "sure" (to turn away). This composition reinforces the idea of complete rupture or liberation.
G0525.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament. In Luke 12:58, Jesus uses it in a concrete judicial context: to release oneself from a lawsuit before the trial. In Hebrews 2:15, its meaning is that of existential liberation — Christ frees from the slavery of fear. In Acts 19:12, it is the diseases that are released from the healed sick. The word always carries a nuance of distancing or separation: something bad moves away.
G0525.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the Gospel truly brings liberation: liberation from the fear of death (Hebrews 2:15), from guilt and slavery. It also invites the Christian to seek reconciliation rather than judicial conflict (Luke 12:58). The healing performed by Jesus in Acts 19:12 shows that this liberation is concrete and visible.

sens: To be excluded from, separated from (that which should belong to us)
To be deprived of access to (a reality, a right, a communion)
To be ignorant of, cut off from (a life, an experience)
G0526.detail:
1. The word describes a separation or exclusion: to be a stranger to something means to be excluded from it, like a stranger who has no place. In Ephesians 2:12, the converted Gentiles remember that they were once "without citizenship in Israel" — they did not belong to the people of God, they were outside. It is the image of a closed door.
2. The word primarily applies to what is spiritual or moral: to be a stranger to something means to have no access to it, to not participate in it. In Colossians 1:21, the Gentiles were "strangers" to the covenants and promises — these did not concern them; they remained a dead letter to them. It is to be cut off from a reality that should nourish our soul.
3. To be a stranger to a life or an experience means to be completely separated from it, ignorant of what it brings. In Ephesians 4:18, being "strange to the life of God" means not living that divine life, not knowing it or sharing it — it is to live as spiritually dead.
G0526.origine: The Greek word is composed of the prefix ἀπ- (ἀπό, "away from, separation") and ἀλλότριος ("stranger, belonging to another"). It thus etymologically means "to make a stranger, to remove from what is one's own." In its Hebrew origin, the word translates זוּר (zûr), which means "to turn aside, to become a stranger." This is the fundamental idea: to move from the status of a member or familiar to that of an excluded or distant one.
G0526.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the passive voice ("to be a stranger to, to be made a stranger to"), designating the state of non-believers or former pagans. It is used in two complementary contexts. First, it describes the legal and religious exclusion of pagans: in Ephesians 2:12, they were strangers to the covenants and promises of Israel — excluded from the divine contract. Secondly, it denotes a moral and spiritual separation: in Ephesians 4:18 and Colossians 1:21, ignorance and sin render humans strangers to the life of God and to His communion. The evangelical context of the New Testament emphasizes that this separation is the fruit of sin and can be overcome by reconciliation in Christ.
G0526.portee: This word helps the Christian reader understand what it means to be separated from God. To be a stranger to His life is to not know Him, to not live in communion with Him: it is the spiritual condition of sin. It also reminds us that the conversion of the pagan to Christ is not a small adjustment, but a radical change of status — from exclusion to acceptance, from ignorance to knowledge. For the believer, this word invites us to measure our own familiarity with God in prayer and Scripture: are we truly close to Him, or do we remain strangers to His life?

sens: Soft, pliable, easy to bend
Newly born or formed, young and fragile
G0527.detail:
1. This word describes what is soft and easy to bend — the opposite of hard or rigid. In the image of the fig tree (Matthew 24:32, Mark 13:28), the branches that become tender in spring are those that have regained flexibility and life after winter: they bend easily under the weight of new leaves. It is a concrete observation that everyone can make: a dead branch breaks, a living branch bends.
2. The word also evokes what is young, fragile, vulnerable — a tender plant, a tender shoot. In the passage about the fig tree, this tenderness of the branches signals the arrival of spring and announces the approaching summer: the tender branches become the living sign that the season has changed. It is a natural clue that Jesus invites His disciples to learn to read as the will of God.
G0527.origine: The Greek word ἁπαλός comes from a root that expresses the idea of soft, pliable. The Hebrew רַךְ ("soft, tender") or the generic sense of what opposes the hard or dry. This family of words always describes what yields easily, what lacks rigidity — tender skin, tender heart, tender flesh.
G0527.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, solely in Jesus' teaching about the signs of the times (Matthew 24:32 and Mark 13:28 are the same passage reported by two evangelists). Jesus uses it to invite His disciples to observe nature as an open book: just as you see the branches of the fig tree becoming tender and understand that summer is approaching, learn to decipher the signs of my coming and the end of the age. The word carries a pedagogical charge here: nature speaks, one only needs to look.
G0527.portee: This word teaches us that God speaks through creation. The tender branches of the fig tree become for the believer a living lesson: to learn to observe, to discern, to read the signs that God places before our eyes. It is an invitation not to be blind to the world around us, but to cultivate a vigilant attention to spiritual realities as we know how to discern natural realities.

sens: to go to meet someone
to find oneself face to face with someone
G0528.detail:
1. The word first expresses the action of going towards someone to meet them, with the intention of joining them. In Mark 14:13, the disciples receive the order: "Go into the city; you will meet a man carrying a pitcher of water" — it is a deliberate walk towards a meeting.
2. The word also designates the moment when two people find themselves face to face, when the meeting occurs. In Luke 17:12, the ten lepers "came to meet him": they walk towards Jesus and there is a meeting between them.
G0528.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "apo" (which means "from, starting from" or "completely") and "antaō" ("to meet", "to go against"). This composition suggests an active meeting, an action of setting out towards each other. In the ancient Greek of the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it generally translates the Hebrew "pagaʿ", which has the same meaning of "to meet" or "to find oneself face to face with."
G0528.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament, both in the accounts of the evangelists Mark and Luke. In Mark 14:13, Jesus sends two disciples to the city promising that they will meet a man with a pitcher — it is a predicted and certain meeting. In Luke 17:12, the ten lepers come to meet Jesus as he enters a village — it is a meeting where the initiative comes from both sides. In both cases, the word describes a real and decisive meeting.
G0528.portee: This word reminds us that meetings in the Gospel are never by chance. When the disciples go to meet this man or when the lepers come to meet Jesus, it is God who guides and ordains these moments. For the believer, this invites us to see every providential meeting as an opportunity where God acts — it is He who organizes our paths.

sens: Action of going towards someone to meet them
The fact of being face to face with a person
Collective movement to welcome someone
G0529.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of heading towards someone, going to meet them. In Matthew 25:6, the virgins go "to meet" the bridegroom: they rise and walk towards him to receive him.
2. It is also the moment when one finds oneself face to face with someone, the point of contact where two movements meet. In 1 Thessalonians 4:17, the Church "to meet the Lord" means that believers rise into the air to go to meet Christ who is returning, and they join him there.
3. The word can also describe a welcome, a collective movement to receive someone of importance. In Acts 28:15, the brothers from Rome come "to meet" Paul at several places: it is an outing to meet him and welcome him with honor.
G0529.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀπαντάω (apantaô), which literally means "to go to meet," formed from the prefix ἀπό (apó, "from" or "against") and the verb ἀντάω (antaô, "to meet"). In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb קָרָא (qara), "to go to meet." The basic image is that of a forward march to join someone who is coming.
G0529.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to denote an outing to meet someone. In Matthew 25:6, it refers to the virgins who rise at night to welcome the bridegroom. In Acts 28:15, it is an honorable welcome reserved for an expected figure. In 1 Thessalonians 4:17, it takes on an eschatological significance (that is, relating to the end times): believers go "to meet" the Lord who descends from heaven. In all cases, the encounter implies a movement towards the one whom we desire to receive.
G0529.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to meditate on vigilance and active waiting. To go "to meet" the Lord is not only to wait for him but to prepare to rise and go towards him. For the Church, this means being in a posture of availability and zeal, ready to welcome the Lord at his coming.

sens: Event that occurred only once in time
Unique moment, without possible repetition
Final accomplishment without need for renewal
G0530.detail:
1. The literal meaning: a unique occurrence of an event. Paul recalls that he was stoned "once" (2 Corinthians 11:25), meaning a single event in his life, at a specific moment in the past. Similarly, the high priest enters the sanctuary "once a year" (Hebrews 9:7), on a single occasion each year.
2. Uniqueness and irreversibility: what will happen only once and cannot be repeated. "It is appointed for men to die once, after which comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27): human death is a unique, inevitable event with no possibility of return.
3. Definitive effectiveness: an act or reality that produces its effect once for all, without needing to be repeated. Christ "offered himself once for all to take away the sins of many" (Hebrews 9:28): this sacrifice does not need to be repeated because it is fully accomplished and sufficient. One who has been purified once (Hebrews 10:2) no longer needs repeated sacrifices to regain purity.
G0530.origine: The Greek word ἅπαξ (hapax) comes from a root meaning "together, at once." It expresses the idea of an action or event that occurs only once, in a single act. In Hebrew, it often corresponds to אֶחָד ("one") or פַּעַם ("time"). The term emphasizes uniqueness and the absence of repetition, making it an important notion to express definitive accomplishment.
G0530.emploi: The word appears about 14 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Epistle to the Hebrews. It can simply describe an event that happened only once in history (Paul stoned once, the high priest entering once a year). But its main meaning in the New Testament, especially in Hebrews, is theological: it expresses the definitive and unrepeatable nature of Christ's sacrifice. Once offered, Christ does not need to sacrifice himself again (Hebrews 9:28; 10:2); this contrasts with the sacrifices of the Old Testament that had to be repeated. This key word teaches that the salvation brought by Jesus is complete and requires no recommencement or supplement.
G0530.portee: This word invites the believer to understand the final power of Christ's sacrifice. Unlike the rituals of the Old Testament, which had to be performed continually, Jesus offered himself once, and that is eternally sufficient. This reassures the Christian: he does not have to save himself and does not have to rely on repeated acts to please God. It is also an invitation to live in the certainty that Christ has completed his work, once for all.

sens: That cannot be violated, infringed, or abolished
That cannot be transferred or passed on to another
That remains unchanging, permanent, eternal
G0531.detail:
1. The word primarily describes something inviolable, which cannot be transgressed or broken: it is a limit or a covenant that no force can cross. It is like a law engraved in stone that no hand can erase.

2. By extension, it means that something cannot be passed on to others, that it cannot be transferred to an heir: it is a charge, a function, or a privilege that remains attached to the one who possesses it and disappears with him. This is the meaning of the unique verse where this word appears: the priesthood of Christ "is not transferable" (Hebrews 7:24), because he alone, living eternally, retains it without interruption.

3. These two meanings converge towards a third idea: invariability, absolute permanence. What is inviolable cannot change; what is inviolable cannot be replaced. It is therefore something stable, eternal, that escapes any alteration.
G0531.origine: The word is composed of α (a-) meaning "not" and παραβάτος (parabaté), "that transgresses" or "that infringes." The root παραβαίνω (parabaïnô) literally means "to walk beside" (παρά = beside, βαίνω = to walk), hence "to transgress, to infringe." Aparabatos thus means literally "that cannot be infringed." In Hebrew, the Old Testament often uses the word bèrit (covenant) with the idea of inviolability: what is inviolable is what cannot be broken or violated, like a covenant established by God.
G0531.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: Hebrews 7:24. In this verse, the Apostle Paul argues that Christ, unlike the priests of the Old Testament who succeeded one another, possesses a "vow" or "inalienable" priesthood — that is, it cannot be transferred to anyone and cannot be replaced. The word contrasts with the hereditary transmission of the Levitical priesthood: where priests succeeded one another, Christ remains "forever" and his priesthood belongs exclusively to him. It is a rare word, chosen to emphasize the uniqueness and immutability of Christ's priesthood.
G0531.portee: This word reminds the Christian that Christ is the permanent High Priest who intercedes eternally for us. We are not left to imperfect successors: it is Christ himself, inviolable and unchangeable, who represents us before God. This truth reassures those seeking lasting assurance in their relationship with God: our salvation rests on something stable, which cannot wear out or be passed on to another.

sens: Who has prepared what is necessary
Who is in a state to receive or act without delay
G0532.detail:
1. The word describes someone who has prepared, who has made the necessary arrangements — it is the opposite of being caught off guard. Paul fears that the Macedonians will arrive among the Corinthians and find them *unready*, that is, without having gathered the collection he organized: this lack of preparation would put them in embarrassment (2 Corinthians 9:4).
2. More broadly, being ready means being in a position to receive, welcome, or face what comes. It is a state of availability: one has planned, one has organized, and therefore can respond without confusion or shame.
G0532.origine: The word is composed of the prefix *a-* (negative) and *paraskevastos*, a participle of the verb *paraskevazo* (“to prepare”). This verb comes from *paraskeuê*, which originally denotes military preparation, the equipment and arrangement of troops before battle — an image of putting in order. The Greek word translates the Hebrew idea of being *prepared*, *disposed* for action or reception.
G0532.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 9:4. Paul mentions his collection for the saints in Jerusalem and his fear that, if the Macedonians join him, they will find the Corinthians unprepared — without the promised offering. The context is pastoral: Paul wants to motivate the Corinthians not to let their generosity fade, and he uses the image of the confusion that would come if they were found lacking. The word emphasizes the importance of vigilance and follow-through in Christian commitment.
G0532.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life requires constant preparation and a genuine willingness to keep one's commitments. Being “ready” is not passivity, but action — preparing, organizing, putting one's heart and actions in order to honor promises to God and to fellow believers. It is an invitation to maturity and reliability in faith.

sens: refuse to acknowledge someone or something
reject, disavow someone
say no to oneself, renounce oneself
abandon faith in someone
G0533.detail:
1. To deny is to refuse to acknowledge something or someone, as if it does not exist or does not matter to you. It is to deliberately ignore, to turn away. Peter denies Jesus when he says, “I do not know him” (Matthew 26:34-35): he refuses to acknowledge that he knows him.

2. The word can also express a disavowal: one denies someone by publicly rejecting them, declaring them untrustworthy. All the uses of deny for Peter show this shameful rejection of Jesus at the time of the Passion (Mark 14:30, Luke 22:34).

3. Applied to oneself, to deny means to renounce one's own interests, to reject selfishness. Jesus calls his disciples to deny themselves: to accept no longer being the center of their lives (Matthew 16:24, Mark 8:34).

4. In the passive voice, the word describes one who is denied, publicly rejected: “Whoever denies me before men, I will also deny before my Father” (Luke 12:9).
G0533.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: ἀπό (“away from, back”) and ἀρνέομαι (“to refuse, deny”). The image is of someone turning away, refusing face to face. In Hebrew, the underlying verb מָאַס also means “to reject, despise.” This word appears only once in the Greek Old Testament (Isaiah 31:7), but the notion of denial runs throughout Scripture when it comes to apostasy or betrayal.
G0533.emploi: The verb appears eleven times in the New Testament, especially in the three synoptic gospels. It carries two distinct meanings. First, it describes Peter's denial: three times before the rooster crows, he refuses to acknowledge Jesus (Matthew 26:34, 35, 75; Mark 14:30, 31, 72; Luke 22:34, 61). These verses report Jesus' words, then the fulfillment of this prophecy. Next, Jesus uses the same verb to call his disciples to deny themselves, to renounce their own will (Matthew 16:24; Mark 8:34). Finally, in the solemn statement of Luke 12:9, Jesus declares that he will deny whoever denies him before men: the word then evokes eternal retribution.
G0533.portee: Peter's denial shows that even the closest to Jesus can fail under fear; but the forgiveness he later receives reveals limitless grace. For the disciple, the call to deny oneself is not a condemnation of life, but an invitation to freedom: ceasing to live for oneself means truly living for Christ and for others. Denying one's selfishness out of love for the Master is to find true life.

sens: action of finishing, bringing to an end
cost or effort necessary to complete a work
G0535.detail: 1. Completion is the action of fully finishing a work that has been started — bringing it to an end. In Jesus' parable (Luke 14:28), he speaks of the completion of a tower one wants to build: one must first calculate the total cost, including what it will take to finish it. 2. By extension, the word also denotes the effort or means — often the cost in money or resources — that must be anticipated and provided for the work to be completely finished. Starting a tower without planning for its completion is to condemn oneself to incompleteness and ridicule (Luke 14:29).
G0535.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb “apartizô,” which means properly “to finish completely” or “to complete.” This verb is formed from the prefix “apo-” (to the end, completely) and a root evoking the limit or extremity of something. The family of this word expresses the idea of reaching the end of an action, a construction, a task, until its total accomplishment.
G0535.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 14:28, in the parable of the one who wants to build a tower. Jesus uses it to teach the importance of reflection and planning: one must calculate whether one has the necessary resources for the complete completion of their project, otherwise one exposes oneself to the public humiliation of an unfinished work. This rare word emphasizes that finishing a work requires counting the cost to the end, including the final step.
G0535.portee: For the believer, this parable invites lucidity and perseverance. Following Jesus is not a light undertaking: one must count the real cost and commit to completion. The disciple must from the outset ask whether he has what it takes to go all the way with this commitment.

sens: The first fruits or products of a harvest, offered to God as a sacrifice
The beginning or the first part of an action or a harvest
What is offered to God to consecrate the rest
Figuratively: the first converts or believers of a region or group
The portion of the Holy Spirit given now to believers, a pledge of the coming resurrection
Christ risen, the first of a harvest of the resurrected
G0536.detail:
1. The firstfruits refer to the first fruits harvested, separated, and offered to God to thank Him (Numbers 15:20 cited in the definition). This act honored God and consecrated the entire forthcoming harvest.
2. Spiritually, the firstfruits of the Spirit (Romans 8:23) are the gift of the Holy Spirit that believers receive now — an advance, a guarantee of the future resurrection of the body. It is like the first fruits that promise the complete harvest to come.
3. The first converts of a region are called firstfruits: Epaenetus is "the firstfruits of Asia" (Romans 16:5), the household of Stephanas "the firstfruits of Achaia" (1 Corinthians 16:15). They are the first to taste the Gospel and in some way consecrate it for the entire region.
4. Christ Himself is "the firstfruits of those who have died" (1 Corinthians 15:20, 23): He is the first resurrected, thus opening the harvest of the general resurrection on the day of judgment.
G0536.origine: The Greek word comes from "apa" (outside, away) and "archē" (beginning, first part). It designates what is separated at the beginning, the first fruits. In Hebrew, the translated word is mainly "térumah" (offering, gift) or "réchit" (first part, beginning), both linked to the idea of a gift that sanctifies the whole. The image is that of a farmer or shepherd offering to God the first results of his work, as an act of consecration and gratitude.
G0536.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles. In Romans 8:23, Paul applies it to the Holy Spirit received now by believers, describing it as an advance on the future resurrection. In Romans 11:16, he applies it to the consecrated dough (the firstfruits of the Jewish people) to say that the rest is sanctified. In 1 Corinthians 15:20-23, Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection, the guarantee that the dead will also be resurrected. Paul also uses it to designate the first converts of a region (Romans 16:5, 1 Corinthians 16:15, James 1:18, Revelation 14:4), always with the sense that they are first and exemplary, consecrating the harvest to come.
G0536.portee: This word teaches the believer that he is never alone in his faith: Christ is "the firstfruits", the first, and each believer is part of the harvest that follows him. The Spirit we have received is "the firstfruits", a pledge that God will keep all His promises of resurrection and transformation. Finally, being "the firstfruits" of a region is to have the privilege and responsibility to show others what the Gospel can do.

sens: The whole, without exception: each part or each element
All members of a group, taken collectively
The totality of a thing, taken as a whole
Each, any element of a set
G0537.detail:
1. The word designates the complete whole, leaving nothing aside. When Luke recounts that John baptized "all" the people (Luke 3:21), it means that no one was excluded. Similarly, "all" who were in the boat (Luke 9:15) represents every person present without exception.
2. It expresses the unanimity or totality of a group of people. In Acts 2:44, "all who believed" refers to the entire body of believers in Jerusalem acting as one: "they had everything in common". It is the whole group, considered at a glance.
3. It can qualify a unique thing taken in its entirety. When the devil shows Jesus "all" the kingdoms of the world (Luke 4:5), the word encompasses the totality of these kingdoms as a single reality. Or again, "all" the people (Luke 20:6), to say the whole people as a block.
4. Rarely, it takes on a nuance of "each" or "any". This meaning is less common than the others and remains close to the idea of exhaustiveness.
G0537.origine: The word ἅπας (hapas) is a reinforced form of πᾶς (pas, "all"). The prefix ἅ- gives it more strength: it is a supported "all", insisting. It is particularly frequent in Luke and Acts, where the author likes to emphasize the unanimity of believers or the totality of an action. This intensification reflects the narrator's concern to show that nothing is left aside.
G0537.emploi: The word appears 34 times in the New Testament, especially in Luke and Acts (more than half of the uses). It can precede the noun ("all men") or follow it, and it is also used alone to designate a group without repeating the name. In Acts, it often emphasizes the unity of the early believers: "all had everything in common" (2:44), "all" were filled with the Holy Spirit (4:31). In Luke, it often depicts universal astonishment at miracles: "all were amazed" (5:26). Matthew uses it less, but it appears in equally decisive contexts, such as the Great Commission: "go, teach "all" nations" (Matthew 28:19 implicit).
G0537.portee: This word reinforces the message that nothing escapes God or the action of His Spirit. When we read that "all" believers were filled with the Holy Spirit, it denies any exception or lukewarmness: it is the whole of the early Church that experienced divine power. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation not to stand aside, but to recognize oneself in the totality of God's people and to fully participate in the common life of believers.

sens: To mislead someone with false or deceptive words
To lead astray regarding the truth or the good
To morally or spiritually mislead
G0538.detail:
1. To deceive is to mislead someone by presenting words or ideas that are not true. In Ephesians 5:6, Paul warns: "Let no one deceive you with empty words", meaning do not be persuaded by empty words that seem beautiful but are hollow.
